evidence.claim: Earlier mountain roads carried timber: Mormon volunteers supplied most of the labor for the Mormon Lumber Road, built up Waterman Canyon in 1852.
evidence.quote: Mormon Lumber Road was built in 1852 up Waterman Canyon

evidence.claim: Mormon volunteers supplied most of the labor
evidence.quote: Most of the labor to build the road came from Mormon volunteers.

evidence.claim: Six sawmills followed at its upper end in 1854, and timber went downhill to help build San Bernardino and other Southern California settlements.
evidence.quote: At the top of the road, they built six sawmills in 1854. The timber was brought down from the San Bernardino Mountains to help build the City of San Bernardino, California and other settlements in Southern California.

evidence.claim: Later, Running Springs developed after state highway improvements in the 1920s.
evidence.quote: The area was developed after improvements to the state highways in the 1920s.

evidence.claim: Lake Gregory filled much faster than its builders expected: three days instead of the estimated three years.
evidence.quote: It had been estimated that it would take three years to fill the lake.  So heavy were the rains that the lake filled in only three days.

evidence.claim: Work to dam the forks of Houston Creek began in 1937 with a Works Progress Administration grant.
evidence.quote: Work began in 1937 under a Works Progress Administration (WPA) grant to dam the east and west forks of Houston Creek

evidence.claim: Federal money ran out before completion, and citrus grower Arthur Gregory lent the district money to finish.
evidence.quote: Gregory financed the completion of the project, lending money to the district for the completion.

evidence.claim: citrus grower Arthur Gregory
evidence.quote: Redlands citrus grower Arthur Gregory, Sr.

evidence.claim: Heavy rain in March 1938 supplied the water.
evidence.quote: The project was nearly completed by March 1938, but federal funds had run out.

evidence.claim: Heavy rain in March 1938 supplied the water.
evidence.quote: Heavy rains that March put the dam to its first test.

evidence.claim: Gregory had also built a sawmill to produce wood for crates for his citrus fruit.
evidence.quote: He erected a sawmill at Valley of the Moon to cut wood for crating his "Orange Blossom" brand of citrus fruit.

evidence.claim: The final part of the project was a road over the dam, completed in January 1939: present-day Lake Drive.
evidence.quote: A road built over the dam (present-day Lake Drive) completed the project in January 1939.

evidence.claim: The locomotives reached the mountains by wagon.
evidence.quote: The Shay locomotives had to be disassembled and hauled by wagon up the mountain

evidence.claim: Brookings Lumber & Box Company operated between Fredalba and Hunsaker Flats, now Running Springs, from 1899 to 1912.
evidence.quote: It operated on 8,000 acres (32 km2) between Fredalba and Hunsaker Flats (present-day Running Springs), and extending northward to Heap's Ranch and Lightningdale (near Green Valley Lake) between 1899 and 1912.

evidence.claim: The railroad had carried logs to Fredalba for milling.
evidence.quote: It built a logging railroad to bring logs to the mill at Fredalba.

evidence.claim: Its logging railroad had no connection to the lowland railways, so the Shay engines were dismantled for the trip uphill.
evidence.quote: since the railroad operated in the high country but did not connect to other railroads in the lowlands.

evidence.claim: About 60 percent of the finished lumber went down steep grades by wagon to Highland’s Molino box factory, which made citrus packing crates.
evidence.quote: About 60% of the finished lumber was hauled by wagon down the steep grades to the Molino box factory in Highland, which made packing crates for the citrus grown in the area.

evidence.claim: In 1912, the company dismantled the Fredalba mill and moved much of its machinery to Oregon.
evidence.quote: In 1912, the company dismantled the Fredalba sawmill and moved much of the machinery to Brookings, Oregon.

evidence.claim: A small road in front of Angelus Oaks Lodge follows the original wagon road.
evidence.quote: The original wagon road is the small road that now runs along the front of the Lodge

evidence.claim: Stagecoaches carried passengers and mail from Redlands through Camp Angelus, as the community was then called, toward Seven Oaks and Big Bear.
evidence.quote: the stagecoach, using the old wagon road, would bring passengers and mail from Redlands up Mill Creek, then Mountain Home Creek (Lower Control Road), through Camp Angelus, on to Seven Oaks via Middle Control Road and then up the back side of the mountain to Big Bear.

evidence.claim: The lodge began as a place to change horses at the top of the climb and serve sandwiches to passengers.
evidence.quote: The now Angelus Oaks Lodge was first built as a stagecoach stop for changing horses at the top of the climb and for serving up sandwiches to passengers.

evidence.claim: The community’s present name came in the 1970s, when the postal service combined the Camp Angelus and Seven Oaks post offices.
evidence.quote: In the 1970s, when the postal service decided to combine the two small post offices of Camp Angelus and Seven Oaks, closing the Seven Oaks location, they renamed the remaining office "Angelus Oaks".

evidence.claim: The wagon road continues from the lodge’s front to the present chain-up turnout, at Middle Control Road.
evidence.quote: The original wagon road is the small road that now runs along the front of the Lodge and crosses over to the current chain up turn-out (Middle Control Road).

evidence.claim: The small road along the lodge’s front follows the original wagon road.
evidence.quote: The original wagon road is the small road that now runs along the front of the Lodge

evidence.claim: The byway is open year-round, but winter snow can make chains necessary.
evidence.quote: This Byway is open year-round, but you may need chains in the winter as this area does receive snow.
